P1.evidence: The best-run open in the batch. Pre-call information was acknowledged up front — 'I already got some information from Trevor' — and then actually used twice as read-backs rather than being left on the shelf: 'I heard from Trevor that you also do some running, right?' and 'More athletic, more defined. That's also what I heard from Trevor.' The frame carried two of four parts with the disqualification promise attached, agreement was sought and given ('Okay?' / 'Yes. Perfect.'), and the open question ran verbatim: 'So take me through, like what can we potentially help you with?' Only P1b holds it back — what's in the way and what you need were never named.

P2.evidence: Six of nine and the strongest injury screening anywhere in this batch. Age was asked and height and weight confirmed from Trevor's notes. Occupation was asked properly and pursued — 'in the go-kart team that you're in, are you the racer yourself or what sort of your position?' — and the travel pattern that drives his nutrition problem came out of it. The injury check ran and then ran twice more with specific hypotheses: first 'do you have some mobility things that you want to work on? Anything that I should know about?', then a targeted runner's-knee probe ('a lot of people that we speak to that have a background in running also get some joints and mobilities in their knees'), then a hips-and-back probe. That is how the check is meant to work. Training week, current results and nutrition were all covered thoroughly, including the go-to off-plan food and its frequency. Health conditions, sleep and energy were never asked; the ten-year cannabis history came out only because the prospect volunteered it twenty minutes later.

P3.evidence: The bridge ran with a proper comparison frame — 'a lot of people would be okay with being in that stage... Why is it important for you, José, to actually get stronger? Is there a deeper reason?' — and produced the tent-and-heavy-equipment answer, which is P3c arriving through P3d. The rep then asked the bridge a second time later in the call ('why is it important for you to take action on it now instead of waiting another few years?') and that second ask is what surfaced the real material: ten years of cannabis use, quitting three to four months ago, and training as the replacement behaviour. He handled it well — 'you're not thinking of even smoking at the time, because you're working out more' — and later used it as the fit argument. Where it stalls: who-else-does-this-impact was never asked despite a wife appearing twice, and the reflect-backs were accurate summaries rather than reframes. Aesthetics was clarified ('What do you mean with your physique?') but treated as secondary, correctly following the prospect's own ordering.

P4.evidence: Complete. The history came out — calisthenics in the park from December, increasing consistency two to three months ago, running — and the failure was traced to a genuinely diagnostic answer: 'with calisthenics, I only have my own body weight... I can't lower the weight. So if I'm not at the starting point, it's like I can't progress.' The root-cause question ran directly — 'what would be the thing for you that we would need to crack in order to actually get to those outcomes?' — and the prospect named the gap himself: 'I think maybe my form, and to make sure that I am working the correct muscles.' P4f drops out as not applicable rather than scoring as a miss: the script's premise is that information is never the problem, and here the prospect's blocker genuinely is technique, with discipline explicitly not an issue — 'I've gotten better with my discipline. I have my workouts more planned.' Running the line would have contradicted the diagnosis.

P5.evidence: Two of four, and the two that ran were run properly. The cost-of-inaction question was specific rather than generic — 'if that keeps on going for another six months, 12 months from now, how would that be when you don't really see a progress... and putting up the tent with work is still the exact same level of how hard it is?' — and drew a real answer: 'That would be demotivating... it would be disappointing.' The settle question followed immediately and was pushed once when the first answer was soft: 'Would that be enough for you? Or would you be like, no, I wouldn't be happy if that would be the outcome in a year from now?' — 'No, no, no, no. I wouldn't be happy.' No why-not and no line in the sand, which is where the frame loses its force: the prospect conceded he would be disappointed, and was never asked to say why it mattered.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran in full after the three pillars and drew the firmest answer in the batch: 'do you feel like if we have all of those three in your life, that is actually going to help you get to the part where you're more stronger, where you get even more healthy... and also where you stay lean?' — 'definitely. I think everything combined will be really good.' The rep also secured a behavioural commitment along the way, which is not in the script but is useful: 'Can you promise yourself also that you're actually going to send him those things and communicate as much as possible?' P6b was again not asked, and again its absence is decisive — 'if you had everything you needed, is there any reason you wouldn't go all in' would have surfaced a two-month income gap and an unquantified tax bill before the price landed rather than after.

P11.evidence: Two closes were attempted and neither collected payment. The $6,000 close was withdrawn by the rep himself on affordability grounds, and the $200 a month close was deferred by the prospect. Onboarding, the agreement and the welcome sequence were never reachable on either path. Not captured by the checks but worth recording: the rep held the price, offered no discount, and voluntarily recommended the cheaper of the two lower-tier options because it can be cancelled.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in this batch. Isolation ran first — 'just a triple check, right? Outside of the investment part, do you feel like, yeah, I do want to get started with this?' — and the should-I-versus-how frame ran in the rep's own words: 'it sounds like it's a, I want to do this, but we just have to figure out the finances, see if we can actually make it work.' Permission for an honest financial conversation was sought ('we can just have a conversation about it, see if we can make something work'). Cash on hand ran and returned a number, month-end surplus ran and returned the key fact that his income is variable with two months of nothing ahead, and credit and third-party financing were raised and then correctly ruled out on residency grounds. Only investments went unasked. The play then did what the play is for: it established that the prospect could not afford it, and the rep acted on that finding rather than against it — 'honestly speaking, I wouldn't advise you to go start with this at the moment, because I don't want to put you in a financial position.'

'I have to think about it here. So I wouldn't say yes right now', on the $200 a month tier. The rep probed four separate times, which is more effort than any other think-about-it in this batch: what he specifically meant, whether waiting six months was worth it physically, what had made him take the meeting at all if he intended to wait, and whether the risk was real. Each probe drew a substantive answer. None of the scripted moves ran — no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here', no identity question — and the rep did not press once the answer turned out to be a two-month income gap and an unknown tax bill. Correct judgement, incomplete play.

'I'd wait until the end of August' is a right-time objection. The rep tested the premise rather than accepting it — 'is it like a real risk that you're taking or what's the reason that you're pushing back to August?' — and got a specific, verifiable answer. He also made a version of the momentum argument on the way out: 'because you have so much time now, in those two months, you can have such a big progression already.' None of the scripted OD moves ran.

Script gap: variable freelance income with a known zero-earning window. The blocker is not capacity to pay in general but timing of cashflow, and nothing in OC or OD addresses it. A start-now-pay-on-invoice structure, a deferred first payment, or a pause mechanism would all be legitimate answers and none exists. Worth logging alongside the international-payment gap from the Georgy call as the same underlying problem: the offer has one payment shape and prospects have many.

Second gap, and a clinical one. The prospect asked twice, in plain terms, whether a week of hamstring pain after his first goblet squats was normal and whether he should push through it — 'I don't know if I did something wrong, and I don't know if I feel this pain, if it's normal, or if I can just push through and keep working out normally.' The rep gave a reasonable heuristic (a day or two is normal, a week is too much, could be form or weight) and then moved on without resolving it. There is no scripted path for a prospect reporting an active, unexplained injury on the call, and the eventual outcome was that he was sent an unsupervised video to follow.

notes: The best-run call in this batch and the clearest evidence that process quality and outcome are separable. Phases 1 through 4 were essentially complete, the injury screening was a model of how the check should work, and the money play ran end to end and produced the right answer. The rep then did the thing worth protecting: he disqualified a prospect he could have pushed, said so plainly, and recommended the cheaper of two lower-tier options because it is cancellable. Two coaching points remain. First, P6b for the fifth time in this batch — a two-month income gap and an unknown tax bill were entirely foreseeable and surfaced only after the price. Second, when a prospect twice asks whether an injury is normal and whether to train through it, that question needs an answer or a referral, not a heuristic followed by a video link.
